title: Headaches, palpitations and a low saturation at 21

source.citation: Ali N, Abughazal M, Honeini R, et al. Recognizing Drug-Induced Methemoglobinemia in the Emergency Setting: A Case of Topical Dapsone Toxicity. Cureus. 2025;17(9):e92342.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Headaches, dizziness and palpitations, now short of breath
presentation.hpi: Two weeks of progressively worsening headaches, intermittent dizziness and palpitations. Over the last three days she has become short of breath, first on exertion and then at rest.
meds: Dapsone 5% gel once daily for the past six months

imaging.finding: Clear lung fields; no consolidation, collapse, effusion or pneumothorax
No filling defects in the central or segmental pulmonary arteries; no pulmonary embolism

diagnosis.primary: Acquired methemoglobinemia caused by topical dapsone

management: High-flow oxygen by alternating Venturi and non-rebreather masks at up to 15 L/min
Methylene blue was not given, although the authors note it is typically indicated for significant methemoglobinemia
outcome: Methemoglobin fell to 1.9% without an antidote; oxygen saturation normal on room air by day 4; discharged on day 6, asymptomatic.
teachingPoints: Pulse oximetry misreads methemoglobin: the SpO2 sits around 85–90% and barely improves with oxygen while the arterial pO2 is normal or high (a saturation gap); co-oximetry confirms.
Dapsone, including the topical gel, benzocaine and lidocaine sprays, nitrites and primaquine are classic oxidant causes.
Stop the oxidant and give oxygen; methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV is the antidote when symptoms are significant or the level is high (commonly above 20–30%), but avoid it in G6PD deficiency.

questions.q: What best explains these oxygenation findings?
questions.extra: Arterial blood gas on high-flow oxygen: pO2 25.9 kPa; co-oximetry oxyhemoglobin 87.6%. Chest radiograph: clear lung fields. D-dimer <150 ng/mL.
options: A right-to-left shunt through a patent foramen ovale
A hemoglobin species that cannot carry oxygen
questions.explanation: A high arterial pO2 with a low measured oxyhemoglobin is a saturation gap: oxygen dissolves normally in plasma but part of the hemoglobin cannot bind it. Shunt, ventilation–perfusion mismatch and hypoventilation all lower the pO2 itself. Co-oximetry names the species; here it was methemoglobin 11.1%.

questions.q: Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Dapsone is a classic oxidant cause of acquired methemoglobinemia, even as a 5% gel used for months; benzocaine and lidocaine sprays, nitrites, nitrates and primaquine are others. Spironolactone does not oxidize hemoglobin.

questions.q: Which antidote is indicated if her symptoms worsen or the methemoglobin level climbs above about 20–30%?
questions.explanation: Methylene blue (1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes) speeds the NADPH-dependent reduction of methemoglobin; avoid it in G6PD deficiency, where it can cause hemolysis. In this case stopping dapsone and giving high-flow oxygen were enough: the level fell to 1.9%.

evidence.quote: A 21-year-old female presented to the emergency department with a two-week history of progressively worsening headaches, intermittent dizziness, and palpitations.
Over the preceding three days, she had also developed exertional dyspnea, followed by resting dyspnea.
Her medical history was notable for obstructive sleep apnea and acne vulgaris
for which she had been using spironolactone
topical dapsone 5% gel once daily for the past six months

evidence.quote: heart rate 134 beats/min, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, temperature 37.4°C, blood pressure 140/92 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 87% on room air
she was alert but in mild respiratory distress
Chest auscultation was clear bilaterally, and no peripheral edema was observed.
revealed type 1 respiratory failure, with a methemoglobin level elevated to 11.1%
Oxygen partial pressure (pO₂) 25.9 kPa
Oxyhemoglobin 87.60%
Total hemoglobin 102 g/L
Lactate 0.7 mmol/L
a D-dimer level of <150 ng/mL
showed clear lung fields with no consolidation, collapse, effusion, or pneumothorax
revealed no filling defects within the central or segmental pulmonary arteries to suggest pulmonary embolism (PE)
Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus tachycardia.
Dapsone was discontinued, and she was managed with high-flow oxygen delivered via alternating Venturi and non-rebreather masks at up to 15 L/min.
Although methylene blue is typically indicated for significant methemoglobinemia, it was not administered in this case.
the final VBG in the medical ward showing a methemoglobin level of 1.9%
By day 4, her oxygen saturation had normalized on room air
She was discharged on day 6, hemodynamically stable and asymptomatic.
